table_path <- function(name) file.path(tables_dir, name)
figure_path <- function(name) file.path(figures_dir, name)

read_csv_required <- function(name) {
  path <- table_path(name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop("Required table is missing: ", path, call. = FALSE)
  }
  utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
}

read_csv_optional <- function(name) {
  path <- table_path(name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
}

fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    NA_character_,
    format(round(as.numeric(x), digits), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  )
}

fmt_count <- function(x) format(as.numeric(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)

show_table <- function(data, caption, digits = 3) {
  print(knitr::kable(data, digits = digits, caption = caption))
}

figure_src <- function(name) {
  path <- figure_path(name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop("Required figure is missing: ", path, call. = FALSE)
  }
  gsub("\\\\", "/", file.path("..", "output", "figures", name))
}

include_figure_grid <- function(files, captions, ncol = 2) {
  if (length(files) != length(captions)) {
    stop("files and captions must have the same length.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  width <- paste0(round(100 / ncol - 2, 1), "%")
  cat('<div style="display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:18px; align-items:flex-start;">\n')
  for (i in seq_along(files)) {
    path <- figure_src(files[[i]])
    cat(
      '<figure style="flex:1 1 ', width, '; min-width:320px; margin:0;">\n',
      '<img src="', path, '" style="width:100%; border:1px solid #ddd; padding:4px; background:white;">\n',
      '<figcaption style="font-size:0.92em; color:#444; margin-top:6px;">',
      captions[[i]],
      '</figcaption>\n</figure>\n',
      sep = ""
    )
  }
  cat("</div>\n\n")
}

emit_code_file <- function(path, language) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop("Required source file is missing: ", path, call. = FALSE)
  }
  cat("```", language, "\n", sep = "")
  cat(paste(readLines(path, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"))
  cat("\n```\n\n")
}

# Abstract

This report presents a fully Bayesian analysis of U.S. residential real-estate listing prices using hierarchical regression models fitted by MCMC. The data contain `r fmt_count(raw_rows)` raw listings from `r raw_states` states and territories and `r fmt_count(raw_zips)` ZIP codes. The modeling frame uses a balanced geographic sample with `r fmt_count(train_rows)` training listings, `r fmt_count(test_rows)` held-out listings, `r selected_states` states, and `r fmt_count(selected_zips)` state-ZIP groups.

Three Bayesian models are compared: a pooled regression (M0), a state random-intercept model (M1), and a heteroskedastic state-ZIP hierarchical model (M2). The selected M2 model has the best DIC (`r fmt_num(m2_row$DIC, 2)`), the lowest held-out RMSE (`r fmt_num(m2_row$RMSE, 4)`), the lowest held-out MAE (`r fmt_num(m2_row$MAE, 4)`), and calibrated 95% predictive coverage (`r fmt_num(m2_row$coverage_95, 4)`). Posterior predictive checks show that M2 reproduces geographic heterogeneity well, with mild over-dispersion in the overall standardized log-price distribution.

# Introduction

## Motivation and goals

Real-estate prices vary with property characteristics such as living area, lot size, bedrooms, bathrooms, and listing status. They also vary geographically: two similar homes can have different listing prices because they are located in different states or local ZIP-code markets. A fully Bayesian hierarchical model is appropriate because it estimates fixed property effects, geographic variation, predictive uncertainty, and partial pooling within one coherent probability model.

The inferential goals are:

1. estimate associations between listing price and measured property features;
2. quantify state-level and ZIP-level residual price variation;
3. compare increasingly structured Bayesian models using DIC and held-out prediction;
4. verify MCMC reliability and simulation-based parameter recovery;
5. evaluate whether the fitted model reproduces relevant observed data features;
6. generate posterior predictive price distributions for interpretable real-estate scenarios.

The geographic parameters are descriptive and predictive associations. The data are observational listings, so the model does not identify causal effects of location, status, or property characteristics.

# Data description and preprocessing

## Source data

The dataset is the USA Real Estate Dataset from Kaggle, version 25, downloaded on 21 June 2026 [@kaggle_us_real_estate]. The raw CSV is preserved locally as `data/raw/realtor-data.csv`, has MD5 checksum `09ce5bd36ef648a5769a996735c05951`, and is excluded from version control.

```{r data-overview}
overview_display <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("Raw rows", "Raw columns", "Unique states/territories", "Unique cities", "Unique ZIP codes"),
  value = c(
    fmt_count(overview_value("rows")),
    overview_value("columns"),
    overview_value("unique_states"),
    fmt_count(overview_value("unique_cities")),
    fmt_count(overview_value("unique_zip_codes"))
  )
)
show_table(overview_display, "Raw dataset overview.")
```

The modeling variables are price, living area, lot size, bedrooms, bathrooms, listing status, state, and ZIP code. Positive price and house size are required because the response and living area enter on the log scale. Lot size uses a `log1p` transformation so that zero-acre listings remain valid while extreme large lots are compressed.

```{r data-dictionary}
dictionary_display <- dictionary[, c("variable", "type", "missing_n", "missing_percent")]
names(dictionary_display) <- c("Variable", "Type", "Missing count", "Missing percent")
show_table(dictionary_display, "Data dictionary and missingness for raw fields.")
```

## Cleaning, transformations, and analysis sample

The response is standardized log listing price. Continuous covariates are also standardized using training-set information. The analysis uses a frozen balanced geographic sample: `r selected_states` states, `r fmt_count(selected_zips)` state-ZIP groups, 30 listings per state-ZIP group before splitting, and a 24/6 train/test split within each group.

```{r row-accounting}
show_table(row_accounting, "Row accounting from raw data to the frozen analysis frame.")
```

```{r data-figure-grid, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(

```

The distribution plots show why modeling directly on the dollar scale would be fragile: both price and size have long right tails. The log transformations reduce extreme leverage while preserving order. The ZIP-count plot also shows that a purely raw-data analysis would be dominated by heavily represented ZIP codes; the balanced sample makes state-ZIP comparisons computationally feasible and more stable for MCMC diagnostics.

# Bayesian statistical models

## Model sequence

The project compares three Bayesian models fit to the same training data:

- **M0: pooled regression.** A common intercept, fixed covariate effects, and a single residual scale.
- **M1: state hierarchy.** M0 plus state-level random intercepts.
- **M2: heteroskedastic state-ZIP hierarchy.** M1 plus ZIP random intercepts nested within states and a residual scale that varies by covariates and state.

For listing \(i\), let \(y_i\) be standardized log price, \(\boldsymbol{x}_i\) be the covariate vector, \(s[i]\) the state index, and \(z[i]\) the ZIP index. The models are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{M0:}\quad y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma), &
\mu_i &= \alpha + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta},\\
\text{M1:}\quad y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma), &
\mu_i &= \alpha + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_{s[i]},\\
\text{M2:}\quad y_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma_i), &
\mu_i &= \alpha + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_{s[i]} + v_{z[i]},\\
&& \log(\sigma_i) &= \gamma_0 + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma} + h_{s[i]}.
\end{aligned}
\]

In M2, \(u_s\) are state deviations, \(v_z\) are ZIP deviations centered within state, and \(h_s\) are state-level residual-scale effects. The sum-to-zero centering makes the intercept identifiable as an overall mean and prevents geographic effects from competing unnecessarily with the intercept.

## Priors and inferential targets

The intercept uses a weakly informative Normal prior centered at zero on the standardized log-price scale. Fixed effects use weak Normal priors, and scale parameters use proper half-Normal priors. The inferential targets are posterior distributions for:

- fixed covariate effects \(\beta\);
- state and ZIP partial-pooling variation;
- residual-scale heterogeneity through \(\gamma\), \(\gamma_0\), and \(h_s\);
- posterior predictive distributions for future listings.

Prior predictive simulation checks whether the model can generate plausible price ranges before seeing the outcome data.

```{r prior-predictive}
prior_settings_display <- prior_settings
show_table(prior_settings_display, "Prior predictive simulation settings.")
```

```{r prior-predictive-figure, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(
  files = c("prior_predictive_price_ranges.png"),
  captions = c("Prior predictive price ranges are compared with observed training prices on the dollar scale."),
  ncol = 1
)
```

The prior predictive plot confirms that the calibrated priors generate broad but interpretable price ranges. This check is important because overly diffuse priors on standardized covariates can produce implausibly extreme dollar prices even before any data are used.

# Simulation-based parameter recovery

The project includes a simulation recovery study in which outcomes are generated from known parameter values and then refit with the Bayesian workflow. This checks whether the computational model can recover parameters under controlled conditions.

```{r recovery-status}
if (!is.null(recovery_status_summary)) {
  show_table(recovery_status_summary, "Repeated simulation recovery completion summary.")
}

recovery_display <- recovery_metrics[, c(
  "label", "true_value", "n_successful_converged",
  "empirical_coverage_95", "posterior_mean_bias", "posterior_mean_rmse"
)]
names(recovery_display) <- c(
  "Parameter", "True value", "Converged fits",
  "Empirical 95% coverage", "Posterior mean bias", "Posterior mean RMSE"
)
show_table(recovery_display, "Simulation recovery parameter metrics.")
```

```{r recovery-figure, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(
  files = c("simulation_recovery_scalar_parameter_recovery.png"),
  captions = c("Scalar parameter recovery compares known simulated values with posterior means and 95% credible intervals."),
  ncol = 1
)
```

The larger reduced-design recovery run completed and converged for all 20 replications. Recovery is strongest for several scale and covariate parameters, while coverage is weaker for some fixed effects. This is not a script failure; it indicates that the reduced simulation design is a stress test and that finite-sample bias or covariate structure can affect interval calibration. The recovery results are therefore interpreted as computational validation with a documented diagnostic caveat rather than as proof that all real-data posterior intervals are perfectly calibrated.

# MCMC computation and diagnostics

The posterior was approximated using four MCMC chains. For the selected heteroskedastic M2 fit, each chain used 2,000 adaptation iterations, 5,000 warm-up iterations, and 10,000 retained sampling iterations, giving 40,000 posterior draws. DIC was computed with a separate lightweight live-JAGS refit because `dic.samples()` requires live model objects rather than saved posterior draws [@spiegelhalter2002bayesian].

```{r mcmc-settings-diagnostics}
m2_settings_display <- m2_settings[m2_settings$setting %in% c(
  "n_chains", "n_adapt", "n_burn", "n_iter", "thin", "seed",
  "chunk_iter", "max_heldout_draws", "max_ppc_draws",
  "sigma_prior_center", "gamma0_prior_scale",
  "gamma_prior_scale", "sigma_state_prior_scale"
), , drop = FALSE]
show_table(m2_settings_display, "M2 MCMC and posterior-check settings.")
show_table(diag_overview, "Numerical convergence and Monte Carlo accuracy summary for M2.")
```

All `r convergence_status$n_parameters` monitored M2 parameters passed the pre-specified convergence checks. The maximum R-hat was `r fmt_num(convergence_status$max_rhat, 4)`, the minimum bulk ESS was `r fmt_num(convergence_status$min_bulk_ess, 1)`, and the maximum MCSE/posterior-SD ratio was `r fmt_num(convergence_status$max_mcse_sd_ratio, 4)`. These diagnostics support using the posterior draws for inference and prediction.

```{r mcmc-diagnostic-grid, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(
  files = c(
    "m2_traceplots.png",
    "m2_rank_histograms.png",
    "m2_acf.png"
  ),
  captions = c(
    "Trace plots should show stable mixing without persistent chain separation.",
    "Rank histograms check whether chains explore the same posterior distribution.",
    "Autocorrelation plots assess dependence between successive MCMC draws."
  ),
  ncol = 3
)
```

The diagnostic plots are read together with the numerical summary. Stable traces, overlapping rank behavior, and acceptable autocorrelation support the conclusion that the MCMC approximation is adequate for the displayed posterior summaries.

# Posterior inference

## Fixed effects and variance components

```{r posterior-summary-tables}
fixed_display <- posterior_fixed[, c(
  "component", "posterior_median", "lower_95", "upper_95", "posterior_probability"
)]
names(fixed_display) <- c(
  "Effect", "Posterior median", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%", "Pr(effect > 0)"
)
show_table(fixed_display, "M2 fixed-effect posterior summaries.")

variance_display <- posterior_variance[, c(
  "component", "posterior_median", "lower_95", "upper_95", "posterior_probability"
)]
names(variance_display) <- c(
  "Quantity", "Posterior median", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%", "Posterior probability"
)
show_table(variance_display, "M2 residual and geographic variation summaries.")
```

The fixed effects have the expected qualitative pattern. Larger living area and larger lot size are associated with higher listing prices, and bathrooms have a clear positive association. Bedrooms have a small negative association after controlling for living area and bathrooms, which is plausible because additional bedrooms at fixed size can reflect smaller rooms or different property configurations. The sold-status coefficient is negative relative to the reference status in this balanced modeling frame.

The posterior median typical residual SD is `r fmt_num(posterior_variance$posterior_median[posterior_variance$component == "Typical residual SD"], 3)`. State and ZIP variation are both substantial, indicating that geographic partial pooling remains important after property features are included.

```{r posterior-figure-grid, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(
  files = c(
    "m2_fixed_effect_forest.png",
    "m2_variance_component_posteriors.png",
    "m2_state_effects_caterpillar.png",
    "m2_selected_zip_effects_caterpillar.png"
  ),
  captions = c(
    "Fixed-effect forest plot: intervals away from zero indicate strong posterior evidence for an association.",
    "Variance-component posteriors: residual, state, and ZIP scales quantify remaining unexplained variation.",
    "State-effect caterpillar plot: state effects are partial-pooling deviations from the overall intercept.",
    "Selected ZIP-effect caterpillar plot: ZIP effects are local deviations centered within states."
  ),
  ncol = 2
)
```

The caterpillar plots should not be interpreted causally. They show residual geographic associations conditional on the included covariates. The hierarchical structure shrinks uncertain state and ZIP effects toward their group-level distributions, reducing instability relative to separate unpooled estimates.

## Posterior predictive scenarios

```{r posterior-prediction-table}
prediction_display <- predictions[, c(
  "scenario_label", "state", "zip_code", "median_price_usd",
  "lower_50_price_usd", "upper_50_price_usd",
  "lower_95_price_usd", "upper_95_price_usd"
)]
names(prediction_display) <- c(
  "Scenario", "State", "ZIP", "Median price",
  "50% lower", "50% upper", "95% lower", "95% upper"
)
show_table(prediction_display, "Posterior predictive dollar-price scenarios.")
```

```{r posterior-prediction-figure, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(
  files = c("m2_posterior_prediction_intervals.png"),
  captions = c("Posterior predictive price intervals include both parameter uncertainty and listing-level residual variation."),
  ncol = 1
)
```

The scenario predictions illustrate the size of geographic effects. A representative home in a high adjusted-price observed ZIP has a much higher posterior predictive median than the same property profile in a low adjusted-price observed ZIP. A new ZIP in the high-price state has a lower and wider distribution than the observed high-price ZIP because its ZIP effect is not observed and must be drawn from the ZIP-level distribution.

# Model comparison

## DIC and held-out predictive performance

```{r model-comparison-table}
comparison_display <- model_comparison[, c(
  "model", "DIC", "delta_DIC", "RMSE", "MAE", "coverage_95", "MLPD"
)]
names(comparison_display) <- c(
  "Model", "DIC", "Delta DIC", "RMSE", "MAE", "95% coverage", "MLPD"
)
show_table(comparison_display, "DIC and held-out predictive comparison.")
```

M2 is clearly preferred. Its DIC is `r fmt_num(m2_row$DIC, 2)`, compared with `r fmt_num(m1_row$DIC, 2)` for M1 and `r fmt_num(m0_row$DIC, 2)` for M0. On the held-out test set, M2 also has the lowest RMSE and MAE and the best mean log predictive density. Its 95% predictive coverage is `r fmt_num(m2_row$coverage_95, 4)`, close to the nominal 0.95 target. The agreement between DIC and held-out predictive performance supports the selected hierarchical structure.

# Posterior predictive model checking

Posterior predictive checks evaluate whether replicated data generated from the fitted model reproduce important features of the observed training data. The chosen checks target central tendency, distributional spread, upper-tail behavior, state medians, and ZIP-level geographic variation.

```{r ppc-table}
ppc_display <- ppc_key[, c(
  "display_statistic", "observed", "replicated_median",
  "replicated_lower_95", "replicated_upper_95",
  "posterior_predictive_tail_probability"
)]
names(ppc_display) <- c(
  "Statistic", "Observed", "Replicated median",
  "Replicated lower 95%", "Replicated upper 95%", "Tail probability"
)
show_table(ppc_display, "Key M2 posterior predictive checks.")
```

```{r ppc-figure-grid, results='asis'}
include_figure_grid(
  files = c(
    "m0_posterior_predictive_checks.png",
    "m1_posterior_predictive_checks.png",
    "m2_posterior_predictive_checks.png"
  ),
  captions = c(
    "M0 posterior predictive checks: the pooled model misses substantial geographic heterogeneity.",
    "M1 posterior predictive checks: state effects improve geography but still understate ZIP-level variation.",
    "M2 posterior predictive checks: geographic variation is well reproduced, while overall IQR and upper-tail spread remain mildly high."
  ),
  ncol = 3
)
```

M2 reproduces the ZIP mean variance closely: the observed value is `r fmt_num(ppc_key$observed[ppc_key$display_statistic == "ZIP mean variance"], 4)` and the replicated median is `r fmt_num(ppc_key$replicated_median[ppc_key$display_statistic == "ZIP mean variance"], 4)`. The overall IQR and 90th percentile remain moderately above the observed values in replicated data. This means the selected model captures the main geographic structure but still slightly over-disperses the marginal standardized log-price distribution. The discrepancy is reported as a model-checking caveat and a direction for future refinement, not as invalidation of the model.

# Discussion

The results support a hierarchical Bayesian model for these real-estate listings. Moving from M0 to M1 improves geographic structure, but the state-only model cannot represent local ZIP-level variation. The heteroskedastic M2 improves both model comparison and held-out prediction while preserving calibrated predictive intervals.

Substantively, living area, lot size, and bathrooms are positively associated with listing price on the standardized log scale. Geographic effects remain important after these property features are included. The posterior predictive scenarios show that location-specific effects can strongly affect predicted dollar prices for otherwise similar representative homes.

The project also illustrates the value of formal Bayesian workflow checks. Prior predictive simulation prevented implausible prior scales, simulation recovery tested computational behavior under known data-generating values, MCMC diagnostics verified numerical reliability, DIC and held-out metrics compared models, and posterior predictive checks identified what the final model reproduces well and where it remains imperfect.

# Conclusion

The heteroskedastic state-ZIP Bayesian hierarchical model provides the strongest and most interpretable analysis among the fitted models. It is preferred by DIC, held-out RMSE, held-out MAE, and mean log predictive density; it has calibrated 95% predictive coverage; and it reproduces geographic heterogeneity well. The remaining over-dispersion in overall IQR and upper-tail checks is a useful diagnostic for future work, especially for richer nonlinear mean structures or more detailed property-quality information.
